passages.text:
The baseline characteristics of the participants are shown in Table 1. A total of 770 (8.7%) of the participants were living with sarcopenia. The mean age of the participants was 39.2 years, and nearly half of the participants (50.4%) were female. A total of 36.8% of the participants were non-Hispanic white. The majority of the participants (83.5%) had a high school education or above, and more than half were married (59.7%). Figure 2 shows the differences in METs across different characteristics between the participants with and without sarcopenia. Total METs, METs for moderate-intensity PA, and METs for vigorous-intensity PA were significantly greater in the non-sarcopenia group than in the sarcopenia group (Fig. 2A-C). After stratification by occupation, the comparison of the METs for recreational PAs between sarcopenia patients and non-sarcopenia patients was similar to the results without stratification (Fig. 2G-I). However, there were no significant differences in total METs for occupational PA or METs for occupational vigorous-intensity PA across the groups of participants with and without sarcopenia (Fig. 2D and F). The cross-sectional associations between different intensities of PA (total, moderate, and vigorous) and sarcopenia are presented in Table 2. In the fully adjusted model, compared to participants without PAs (METs were 0), participants in the “low”, “moderate”, and “high” total METs groups had lower risks of sarcopenia (low: OR = 0.730, 95% CI: 0.583; 0.915, _p_ -value = 0.006; moderate: OR = 0.643, 95% CI: 0.485; 0.853, _p_ -value = 0.002; high: OR = 0.560; 95% CI: 0.457; 0.687, _p_ -value < 0.001). The stratified analysis of the associations between moderate- or vigorous-intensity METs and sarcopenia also yielded results similar to those of the non-stratified analysis. Table 3 shows the association between the intensity of occupational and recreational PA and sarcopenia. According to the fully adjusted model, the participants in the “high” total METs group had a significantly lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.789; 95% CI = 0.653; 0.954; _p_ -value = 0.014). Similarly, “high” METs for moderate-intensity occupational PA were associated with a lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.797, 95% CI: 0.649; 0.980, _p_ -value = 0.031); however, higher METs for vigorous-intensity occupational PA were not associated with sarcopenia compared to the reference group. A higher intensity of recreational PA was associated with a lower risk of sarcopenia, i.e., the participants who were labeled with “low”, “moderate” and “high” total METs for recreational PA had a decreased risk of sarcopenia (low: OR = 0.758, 95% CI: 0.623; 0.921, _p_ -value = 0.005; moderate: OR = 0.725, 95% CI: 0.553; 0.950, _p_ -value = 0.020; high: OR = 0.444, 95% CI: 0.327; 0.604, _p_ -value < 0.001) compared to the reference group. Figure 3 shows the dose-response relationships between different categories of PA intensity and sarcopenia. The relationships between total METs, vigorous-intensity METs and sarcopenia showed a nonlinear U-shaped trend (Fig. 3A and C). However, the relationship between moderate-intensity METs and sarcopenia revealed an L-shaped nonlinear trend. After stratifying PA by occupational and recreational type, the relationships between occupational moderate- and vigorousintensity PA and sarcopenia showed shapes similar to those of the unstratified relationship, whereas the nonlinear trend became nonsignificant (Fig. 3E and F). Forest plots were drawn to show the associations between different categories of PA intensity (i.e., total METs, occupational PA, recreational PA) and sarcopenia stratified by sex, ethnicity, education, marital status, and poverty status (Fig. 4). Stratified analysis revealed that male, education level of high school and above, and marital status were more likely to reduce the risk of sarcopenia at higher total METs for PA, as shown in Fig. 4A. According to the analysis of the association between occupational PA and sarcopenia, higher total METs for occupational PA did not reduce the risk of sarcopenia in most of the subgroups (Fig. 4B). However, higher total METs for recreational PA significantly decrease the risk of sarcopenia in many subgroups (Fig.4C). For example, married participants who were categorized as having “low”, “moderate” or “high” METs for recreational PA had a lower risk of sarcopenia than did the reference group (low: OR = 0.692, 95% CI: 0.540; 0.888, _p_ -value < 0.05; moderate: OR = 0.664, 95% CI: 0.470; 0.937, _p_ -value < 0.05; high: OR = 0.428, 95% CI: 0.287; 0.637, _p_ -value < 0.05). The results of the sensitivity analysis obtained from the imputed data were consistent with the results of the main analysis. The second method of sensitivity analysis, which included three categories of alcohol consumption (never, every day, and not every day) instead of the dichotomous variable (not drinking, drinking), also showed similar results (Supplemental Table 3). Compared to the participants without any PAs (METs were 0), the participants in the “moderate” and “high” total MET groups had lower risks of sarcopenia (moderate: OR = 0.639, 95% CI: 0.464; 0.881, _p_ -value < 0.01; high: OR = 0.579, 95% CI: 0.460; 0.728, _p_ -value < 0.001). Supplemental Table 4 shows the association between the intensity of occupational and recreational PA and sarcopenia. In the fully adjusted model, the participants in the “high” total occupational MET group had a significantly lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.777, 95% CI: 0.631; 0.957; _p_ -value = 0.018). For moderate-intensity occupational PA, the “high” group had a lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.757, 95% CI: 0.602; 0.952; _p_ -value = 0.017).

passages.heading: **Discussion**
passages.text:
This study investigated the associations between PA intensity, occupational engagement, and sarcopenia among younger adults by using a nationally representative sample from the USA. The findings of the current study indicated that a greater intensity of PA was associated with a lower risk of sarcopenia, with vigorous and moderate PA exhibiting a similar benefit on sarcopenia. Interestingly, more intensive recreational PA was related to a lower risk of sarcopenia; however, no beneficial influence was found on occupational PA. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to investigate the relationships among activity intensity, occupational nature, and sarcopenia among adults. Although the evidence was based on an observational study with a crosssectional design, it can also provide clues for developing more precise PA recommendations for adults for the early prevention of sarcopenia in adulthood. Accumulating literature suggests that engaging in more intensive PA may lower the risk of sarcopenia [41-45], which is in line with the findings of the present study, although some studies have drawn inconsistent conclusions, which may be due to different measurements or diagnostic criteria used [46, 47]. PA may increase the levels of hormones such as testosterone [48] and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) [49] which promote muscle buildup, inhibit TNF-α and other various molecular mechanisms to promote mitochondrial metabolism, upregulate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α (PGC-1α) and downregulate Tolllike receptors, which enhances anti-inflammatory and anti-atrophic functions in skeletal muscle [50]. Moreover, PA can also stimulate phosphatidic acid, which may activate protein synthesis and inhibit autophagy to Page 8 of 12 Zhao _et al. Notably, the risk of sarcopenia decreased if a certain intensity of PA was reached, regardless of whether vigorous or moderate PA was taken; however, it may be difficult for individuals to benefit from extremely intensive PA. The possible reason may be muscle impairment and growth restriction due to overuse of exercise [52]. Regardless of the general benefit of PA, the protective role seems to exist only in recreational activities, which is consistent with previous studies [53, 54]. In contrast, occupation of PAs was not associated with sarcopenia. High labor-intensity PAs may generate physical and mental stress, which may adversely affect muscle function as a result of low autonomy and inflexible working hours [27], leading individuals to fail to meet their muscle mass maintenance needs [55]. Additionally, individuals who engage in occupational PA may tend to have relatively lower socioeconomic status and be exposed to a wide range of adverse work environments [27], which increases their vulnerability to adverse health outcomes. For example, individuals who have a manual occupation usually have an elevated risk of mortality [56], hospitalization for influenza [57] and cognitive impairment [58]. Further research is needed to determine the associations between PA and sarcopenia among adults with physically demanding work. Page 9 of 12 Zhao _et al. BMC Public Health_ (2024) 24:3179 **==> picture [480 x 316] intentionally omitted <==** **Fig. 3** Dose-response relationship between different categories of PA intensity and sarcopenia The current study also revealed that some demographic factors may modify the associations between PA and sarcopenia; for instance, males and individuals with relatively high educational levels seemed to benefit more from being physically active, which is consistent with previous studies [59]. Individuals with different sociodemographic characteristics may have different PA engagement patterns; for example, females are more likely to participate in physical activity in their leisure time [55]; however, males with low incomes (who are closely connected to those with low education levels) are predominantly engaged in physically demanding work. The modification effects of some sociodemographic factors make it difficult to interpret the findings, so future studies should enroll individuals with different sociodemographic characteristics to further verify the findings. This study has the following advantages. First, a nationally representative sample with a large sample size was used for the analysis so that the scientificity and reliability of this study could be guaranteed. Second, sarcopenia was defined by the use of authoritative diagnostic criteria, and limb muscle mass was objectively measured, which was helpful for reducing misclassification bias. Additionally, multiple covariates were included in this study to minimize the interference of confounders. However, there are still some limitations in this study. First, the cross-sectional study design made it unable to determine any causal relationship between PA intensity, occupational engagement, and sarcopenia. Prospective cohort studies are needed to verify the findings of the present study. Second, information on PA was self-reported, which made it impossible to completely avoid reporting bias. Third, only the ratio of ALM to BMI based on the measurement of muscle mass was considered in the definition of sarcopenia in the present study [8, 60, 61]. Since muscle function data (e.g., gait speed) were not available in the NHANES, more comprehensive criteria, such as the EWGSOP and AWGS, could not be applied in the current study. Future studies should include more measurements and further verify the findings obtained from the current study. Additionally, some factors that may potentially impact our findings could not be fully considered because such data were restricted or missing. Hence, such limitations should be considered in future studies; for example, personal medication and employment type should be included in the future study design. Finally, the samples used in the study were predominantly European and American, so the conclusions might be difficult to generalize to other populations. Page 10 of 12 Zhao _et al.
